title: Week 9 · update for the Nov 10 meeting, plus Nov 11 follow-up
sub: LIBERO moka pots (libero_10 task 8): work since the Nov 3 check-in (Nov 4–9), and, in the section under the summary, what I did with the Nov 10 feedback. Advantage-conditioned fine-tuning of π₀.₅, RECAP-style.
goal: **Goal.** Fine-tune π₀.₅ with a RECAP-style advantage tag ("this action was better / worse than usual", from a learned value function) and beat the base policy on one LIBERO task.

summary.t: **A fine-tune recipe that keeps base performance.** Fine-tuning on our rollouts used to cost ~13–16 points. Making demos 75% of the training frames and using a 10× lower learning rate scored **53.6% vs base 52.4%** (one seed; step 2000).

**The advantage tag is still (almost) unused, and the reason is the labels, not the model.** A planted tag of RECAP's expected size is learned on every route, so the conditioning works. Our labels only support a tiny tag-dependent action difference. Changing the value function does not help, and collecting more rollouts from the same policy does not help either: the policy's own data has little better-vs-worse action contrast.
**Best result so far: advantage weighting on the successful rollouts, 56.7%** (+4.2 points; 95% CI −3.0 to +11.5, so not yet different from base).

story.t: **Starting point (week 8 page).** Fine-tuning hurt (base 56.4% → ~41%, older eval settings), and the tagged policy ignored its tag, even when the tag was the true outcome. Two problems: the fine-tune costs performance, and the tag is not learned.

**Fine-tune cost.** Successes only + frozen vision encoder, or a 10× lower learning rate, brought success back to ~52–55%. The training seed alone moves success by ~10 points (same recipe: 63.9% vs 51.8%), so every recipe now needs 2 seeds.
**Closing the gaps to RECAP** (list below). After each fix, flipping the tag still moved the action by only ~1.3–1.9% of the policy's own sampling noise.
**Can the model learn a tag at all? Yes.** A planted tag that shifts the action by RECAP's expected amount is learned on the prompt route and on the AdaRMS route (0.36× noise).

**Are our labels informative? Barely.** An offline test (the "coach test") fits the best possible tag-conditioned action model to our data: our labels support an action difference of 0.015 vs 0.004 for random labels and 0.05 for a positive control. Mostly gripper timing.

**Is the value function the problem? No.** A TD critic, a ResNet + π₀.₅ ensemble, longer lookaheads, hindsight returns and the episode outcome all give weaker labels than the current ResNet. Ground truth from the simulator (restore the state, run 12 continuations) shows the true advantage is itself mostly noise; our labels agree with it only weakly (r = 0.11).

**Is it the amount of data? No.** As episodes grow from 112 to 900, the labels' action information levels off by ~450 episodes, while a real signal (the positive control) keeps rising. A round of rollouts with 2× exploration noise adds only a little.

**Where the fine-tune cost comes from.** Training untagged on all rollouts (successes + failures), as RECAP does, drops success to 39.1%: the failure data causes the earlier drop. Tags or advantage weights recover part of it (40.9–52.4%), but not past base. Raising the demo share and lowering the learning rate is what brought it back to base.

gaps.did: Ours was 70% positive (I had misread RECAP's threshold); switched to 40%. Also tried RECAP's single threshold and a per-round threshold.
gaps.result: Rules give the same label signal (0.016–0.019).

gaps.did: Added the 29 task demos tagged "+", then raised them to 50–75% of training frames.
gaps.result: Helps the fine-tune cost, not the tag.

gaps.did: Built π*0.6's FAST-token loss with stop-gradient, plus subtask text in the prompt ("RECAP-complete").
Pre-trained a "speed" tag on demos of all 40 LIBERO tasks, then fine-tuned.
ResNet-18, out-of-fold; tried a π₀.₅ value expert, a TD critic, an ensemble and subtask-scoped values.
Sim only: a round with 2× exploration noise; branching from saved failure states.
gaps.result: Small gain; branching too noisy at 12 continuations.

discrepancies: **The AdaRMS tag is not fully ignored.** With real labels, flipping the AdaRMS tag moves the action by 0.0060 (13.6% of noise), about 40% of what the labels can support and ~8× the prompt-route runs (0.0008); its training loss is also ~1% lower with the correct tag. Earlier summaries said "tag ignored on every route". That is true for the prompt routes, not for AdaRMS. Its eval with the + tag was 40.9%; it was never evaluated with the − tag, so we do not know if this learned shift changes success.

**The data-curve rule I set used the wrong metric.** I first read "flat" from the ideal shift, but the ideal shift stays flat with more data even for the positive control (it measures effect size, not learnability). The right read is action information: the labels level off by ~450 episodes while the positive control keeps rising. Same conclusion, better reason.

**Eval noise is ±5 points.** Base π₀.₅ scored 56.4% under the older eval settings and 52.4% under the current ones (matched noise); one success-only checkpoint scored 52.1% and 55.5%. One run (demos 75%, low lr) scored 53.6% at step 2000 and 47.0% at step 5000.
**The prompt-route models react to whether the tag text is there, not to its value.** Removing the tag moves the action ~6× more than flipping + to − (0.0045 vs 0.0008).

**Branching: the sim restore was not exact at 25% of branch points** (state difference > 1e-3). The results are unchanged when those points are dropped (true-advantage reliability 0.33, label correlation 0.14).
questions: **More rollouts from the same policy don't help.** The labels' action information levels off by ~450 episodes, and 2× exploration noise adds little. The ground truth from branching suggests why: in most states the policy's actions barely change the outcome. So the limit seems to be the *kind* of data, not the amount. Is a sim version of RECAP's corrections worth building, i.e. actions the policy wouldn't take itself, such as demo-style recoveries from saved failure states? Or should I accept that this setup can't test the tag?
Weighting and filtering give my best numbers so far. Should I lean into advantage-weighted training and treat the tag as secondary?
RECAP learns the tag across many tasks. Is a small multi-task test (a few LIBERO-10 tasks) worth the compute?
The AdaRMS route did learn ~40% of the label signal. Worth a − tag eval of that run (one job) before dropping the tag?
On the value side, I plan to score the ResNet and the truncated π₀.₅ value against the sim ground truth. Is that a good use of time compared with the policy questions?
With ~10-point seed noise, how many seeds would you want before trusting a ~5-point effect?

policy.title: Policy success: what costs performance and what brings it back
policy.question: Change in success vs base π₀.₅ (52.4%) on the same 330 trials (10 held-out scenes × 33, matched noise), paired by trial. Bars are 95% CIs; a bar crossing the dashed line is not distinguishable from base.
verdict: **Failure rollouts cause the drop:** untagged on all rollouts = −13.3 points; on successes only = +3.0.
**More demos + 10× lower lr brings all-rollout training back to base** (demos 75%, low lr: +1.2 at step 2000). Single seed, and the same run is −5.5 at step 5000.
**Tags do not beat base on any route**; advantage weights on all rollouts reach base exactly (+0.0).
**Success-only + weights is the best so far (+4.2)**, still within noise.

tag-effect.title: Does the tag change the action?
tag-effect.question: Flip the tag (+ vs −) with the same sampling noise and measure how far the executed action moves, as a share of how far it moves between two noise draws (1.0 = as much as the policy's own randomness). Final checkpoints.
verdict: **Real labels on the prompt route: 1.3–1.9%**, the same as the oracle outcome tag (1.7%) and no more than a model that never saw a tag (2.4%).
**A planted tag of RECAP's expected size is learned (36–37%) on both routes**, and a large one at 164%. The conditioning works.
**AdaRMS with real labels: 13.6%**, partly learned (see the discrepancies).
For scale: swapping the task instruction moves the action 98% of noise, so the policy does read its prompt.

coach.title: How much could the action depend on the tag, given the labels? (coach test)
coach.question: Fit the best tag-conditioned action model f(state, tag) on the rollouts and measure how much its action changes between + and −. This is an upper bound on what a policy could learn from those labels. Random labels give the floor.
verdict: **Current labels: 0.015, vs 0.004 for random.** The trained prompt-route policies learned 0.0008 of it (5%), AdaRMS 0.0060 (40%).
**No other value function does better:** TD critic 0.013, ensemble 0.012, outcome 0.011, longer lookaheads 0.009–0.010, hindsight 0.009.
**Label rules barely matter** (0.016–0.019), and the exploration round is only slightly above round 1. The PC1 control (a label that truly predicts the action) sits at 0.05–0.06.

curve.title: Would more of the same data help? The data curve
curve.question: Subsample 56–900 episodes (spread evenly over scenes, 5 draws each) and measure how much the action predicts the tag beyond the state (action information, held out). A real signal (PC1 control) should keep rising with data.
verdict: **The positive control keeps rising** (old data 0.03 → 0.17; with exploration rounds 0.10 → 0.23).
**Our labels level off by ~450 episodes** (0.04 → 0.07; 0.06 → 0.08).
So collecting more rollouts of the same kind is unlikely to make the tag learnable. Points at 450 (old) and 900 (pooled) are single draws.

branching.title: Ground truth from the simulator: when is a failure decided?
branching.question: For 12 failed rollouts, restore the exact sim state every 20 steps and run 12 fresh continuations of the base policy. V* = share that succeed (the true chance of success at that moment). The strip under each plot shows the label our pipeline gave that moment (+ or −).
verdict: **The true chance of success is measured reliably:** V* split-half 0.90. In these examples a failure is decided at a few moments: V* falls from ~0.6–0.8 to ~0 within 1–4 branch points (20–80 steps).
**The true advantage is mostly noise:** A* split-half reliability 0.33 (0.50 for all 12 continuations).
**Our labels agree with it only weakly:** correlation with A* 0.11; 37% of moments with A* > 0 are labelled +, vs 23% with A* < 0.
So branching-based corrections would need many more continuations, and only at the decision moments.

minor.title: Label-rule bug: 70% of frames were labelled positive
minor.oneline: RECAP's "30% threshold" had been read as the 30th percentile. Fixed to 40% positive (RECAP fine-tuning), value-binned.
verdict: Literature review of RECAP App. A–F: ~30% positive in pre-training, ~40% in fine-tuning, 30% tag dropout, demos tagged +.
Value-binned calibration (Dissecting, arXiv 2609.28161) removes a V-dependent bias; agreement with a second value model κ 0.20 → 0.29.

minor.title: Tag predictability: the action barely predicts the label
minor.oneline: Knowing the action explains 3–9% of the label's uncertainty beyond the state (stall control 13%, random 0).
verdict: RCSL theory: a tag is ignored when P(tag | state, action) ≈ P(tag | state). That is close to our case.

minor.title: Stopping early is not a fix; seed noise is ~10 points
verdict: The two seeds also succeed on different scenes (scene 48: 88% vs 36%).
Since then: 2 seeds before reading any recipe effect ≤ 10 points; matched-noise evals (same sampling noise per trial) to tighten paired comparisons.

minor.title: Exploration-noise pilot
minor.oneline: 2× sampling noise on some action chunks: success 56.7% vs 64.4% control, 1.64× more spread between rollouts. Chosen for a 450-episode round.
verdict: The 450-episode round: success 60.9%; its labels carry only slightly more signal than round 1 (coach chart).

minor.title: Steering by picking the best of π₀.₅'s action samples
minor.oneline: Even with the simulator as judge, best of 8 gains +0.6 points (CI −2.8 to +4.2); also null at 1.5× and 2× noise.
verdict: The policy's own samples are too alike to choose between: the same low-headroom story as the labels.

since.title: Since Nov 10: feedback and new experiments
since.lead: The Nov 10 feedback asked whether the learned advantage is informative at all, suggested two directions (run an existing RL baseline on this task; read and implement the Advantage Guidance paper), and asked about determinism, retries, more noise, more rounds and seeds. What came of each is below. Every success number is the same 330 held-out trials as base (52.4%), paired by trial, 95% CI.

headline.t: **Advantage Guidance's contrastive guidance is the first arm that beats base: 65.8% vs 52.4%, +13.3 points [+7.0, +19.7]**, with no extra training. It samples the AdaRMS-tag checkpoint as v_ref + w·(v₊ − v₋) at w 8. Success rises with w and the sign flip hurts (w −4: 23.0%). So the tag did learn a small real direction; plain + sampling just under-weights it.
**Caveats on that number:** w was chosen on these same 330 trials, it is one training seed, and the shuffled-label control (is it advantage, or just "look like the demos"?) is still running.

**Residual vs DSRL on the same 330 trials: 75.4% vs 67.9%, +7.6 points [+1.2, +13.9]** (paired by start state and repeat; DSRL picks its own start noise, so it does not share the matched noise seed). Both are one seed.

**Other questions from the feedback:** more exploration noise breaks the policy (3× → 28%, 5× → 0%); learned advantages track the simulator's true advantage at only 0.04–0.14 (ceiling 0.69); the round-1 filtered-BC policy is no better than base on the states it collected (57.6% vs 59.8%), and round 2 (seed 1) does not climb: 50.6% vs round 1's 55.5%.

**Rollout gallery (new):** base vs residual + guidance on the same 330 trials, side by side. Guidance fixes 113 trials and breaks 37; successes are 12 steps shorter on trials both solve [−20.6, −3.9]; most guided failures already have the first pot on the stove.

lars.ask: Is the policy nearly deterministic? Are some start states never solved?
lars.did: Read the existing evals per start state.
lars.result: Not deterministic: success per state 12–91% (val) and 13–93% (train). Every state succeeds sometimes.

lars.ask: Retry from failed states: does every failure have a success nearby?
lars.did: Used the failure-branching runs: 12 continuations from points along 12 failed episodes.
lars.result: Early in a failed episode, success is still 17–83% likely. Later, most episodes pass a point of no return (steps 80–440). 50% of points uncertain, 42% none succeed, 8% all succeed. A dedicated retry-until-success eval was not run.

lars.ask: More exploration noise (2× may not be enough)
lars.did: Swept start-noise scale 2×, 3×, 5×, 8×, and 2× on every chunk; 90 episodes each on train states.
lars.result: 64% (no extra noise) → 57% (2×) → 28% (3×) → 0% (5×, 8×): actions break before they become useful variety.

lars.ask: Keep successes and retrain for several rounds: does it approach 100%?
lars.did: Filtered BC round 2: 900 rollouts with the round-1 policy (30 train states × 15 + 450 fresh layouts), retrain from base on all round-1 + round-2 successes, 2 seeds.
lars.result: Seed 1 done: round 2 gets **50.6% (final), −1.8 vs base [−8.5, +4.8] and −4.8 vs round 1's 55.5% [−11.2, +1.5]**; its step-2000 checkpoint is worse (39.7%). The round-1 policy also collected at 57.6% vs base 59.8% on the same train states, so it was not better where it trains. Seed 0 evals rerunning. So far, no climb toward 100%.

lars.ask: Is the learned advantage informative? If so, why doesn't it show up in the other methods?
lars.did: Scored every value function and label set against the simulator's true advantage (424 branch points).
lars.result: Barely: corr(learned A, true A) 0.04–0.14, against a ceiling of 0.69 set by the ground truth's own noise. But guidance (above) shows the AdaRMS tag picked up a small direction that does help once amplified.

lars.ask: Advantage weighting: good for debugging, not convinced as a method
lars.did: Kept it as a baseline; the follow-up runs finished.
lars.result: Success-only weights on the 75%-demo recipe: 59.4% at step 2000 (+7.0 [+0.9, +13.0]), 55.5% at the end. Same tag model sampled − (59.1%) is not worse than + (57.0%): the prompt tag is still ignored.

lars.ask: Direction 1: run an existing RL baseline on this task to calibrate
lars.did: DSRL (Wagenmaker et al., CoRL 2025), online: π₀.₅ frozen, a small pixel SAC agent picks its start noise. Same task, same 30 train states.
lars.result: Running. See the DSRL chart: flat near base for ~400 episodes, then rising in the latest cycles.

lars.ask: Direction 2: the Advantage Guidance paper (why the policy ignores conditioning; implement it)
lars.did: Read the paper and code. Ran contrastive guidance on the existing tag checkpoint (zero training), built the residual parameterisation, and planned action imagination behind a gate.
lars.result: Guidance w 8: +13.3 points. Residual at the same action shift: +23.0 points (75.4%), +9.7 [+3.0, +16.7] above AdaRMS w 8 on the same trials. Imagination: not built (needs a critic that can rank π₀.₅'s own samples).

lars.ask: Value vs sim ground truth: quick, inference-only signal
lars.result: See the advantage row above; V vs true V* is also weak (0.22–0.29).

lars.did: Seed 1 of the 75%-demo recipe; round 2 trains 2 seeds.
lars.result: Seed 1: 49.7% at step 2000, 53.9% at the end (seed 0: 53.6%, 47.0%). The guidance result is still one training seed.

ag.title: Advantage Guidance (Zhou & Levine): contrastive guidance and the residual parameterisation
ag.question: At sampling time, each denoising step uses v = v_ref + w·(v₊ − v₋): the + and − tag velocities of the same model, with the no-tag branch as v_ref. w scales a direction the model already learned; nothing is retrained. The residual model keeps π₀.₅ frozen as v_ref and adds a small, zero-initialised tag-conditioned head; residual and AdaRMS are compared at the same action shift, not the same w (w means different amounts in each). Change in success vs base on the same 330 trials.
verdict: **w 8 = 65.8%, +13.3 points [+7.0, +19.7]; 8 of 10 start states improve.** Still above zero when resampling whole start states (+0.6 to +25.8).

**Dose-response:** w 2 and w 4 are below base, w 8 above it, and pointing the guidance the wrong way (w −4) costs 29 points. The checkpoint's own reference (w 0) is 13.9 points below base, so w 8 is worth ~27 points relative to it.

**Why w 8 and not the paper's 1–4:** the paper's theorem makes w an inverse temperature (1/β = w·[T(y₊) − T(y₋)]). Our labels are weak (corr 0.10 with the true advantage), which flattens P(+ | A), so a larger w is needed for the same tilt [our reading].
**Open:** w was chosen on these trials; one training seed; the shuffled-label control decides whether the direction is advantage or demo-vs-rollout.

dsrl.title: DSRL online: an established RL method on the same task (suggested direction 1)
dsrl.question: DSRL keeps π₀.₅ frozen and trains a small pixel SAC agent to choose the flow model's start noise (one 32-d vector per chunk), from sparse success reward, online. Paper settings (UTD 20, 10 Q heads, discount 0.999). Points = training success over one cycle through all 30 train states (30 episodes), with the agent's own exploration noise on.
verdict: **Flat near base for ~400 episodes, in both agent lives.** The job was preempted at episode 443 and restarted with a fresh agent (its replay buffer is in memory only).
**Then rising:** both lives start climbing at about the same point (cycle 13). The restarted agent's last 3 cycles average {last3} vs base {base} on the same states.

**Held-out result:** a snapshot saved at episode 971 (about 530 episodes into life 2, early in the rise) gets **67.9% vs base 52.4% on the 330 held-out trials, +15.4 points [+8.5, +22.1]**. The points here are training episodes on the train states with exploration noise on, so they are not comparable with that number. Still one seed; a resumable second seed is next.
dsrl.source: `runs/dsrl_s0_libero_10_18434524/episodes.csv`; base = round-1 rollouts of base π₀.₅ on the same 30 states (`stage2_moka_18155849`, 450 episodes); `reports/2026-11-10-dsrl-online/report.md`

followup.title: Follow-ups on the recipe that kept base (demos 75%, 10× lower lr)
followup.question: The decision job picked the best recipe from the grid and trained three runs on it: seed 1, the RECAP tag (prompt route, dropout 0.3), and success-only advantage weights. Change in success vs base on the same 330 trials.
verdict: **The recipe sits at base ± noise:** seed 1 is 49.7% / 53.9% (step 2000 / end), seed 0 was 53.6% / 47.0%.
**The prompt tag is still ignored:** the same model sampled with − (59.1%) does slightly better than with + (57.0%).

**Success-only weights at step 2000: 59.4%, +7.0 [+0.9, +13.0]**, the best fine-tune so far, but 55.5% at the end, and +7.0 [−3.9, +15.2] when resampling start states. Treated as a baseline, as suggested.

other.title: Other checks: exploration noise, value vs ground truth, round-2 collection
other.question: Three quick checks from the feedback.
verdict: **More noise breaks the policy before it adds useful variety** (3× → 28%, 5× → 0%).
**Every learned advantage tracks the true advantage weakly** (0.04–0.14), well below what the noisy ground truth allows (0.69). Random labels: 0.01.
**The round-1 filtered-BC policy is not clearly better than base where it collects** (unpaired, about ±3 points).

Its + vs − difference is ~1% of noise, so guidance should do nothing there.

ask: Guidance beats base, and the residual parameterisation goes further (75.4%, above DSRL's 67.9%). Is this the direction to push (seeds, fresh trials, the anchor test), or does it change the RECAP question?
Which to prioritise for GPUs: confirming guidance, scaling DSRL (seeds, held-out eval), or the residual / imagination line?
DSRL reaches 67.9% on the held-out trials after ~1000 episodes. Is it worth more seeds as the RL baseline, or is one run enough to calibrate against?
